slides.title: What is money?
slides.text: Money is a tool people use to pay for things. If an apple costs $1, you can give the store $1 and take the apple home. Money helps us trade without having to swap one thing for another.

widgetConfig.scenario: An apple costs $1. How can you get the apple without trading something else for it directly?

options.label: Give the store $1
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money is a tool people use to pay for things — you give the store $1 and take the apple home.

options.label: Trade your shoes for it
options.outcome: Trading your shoes isn't how money works — giving the store money lets you avoid swapping other things directly.

options.label: Money cannot be used to pay for things
options.outcome: Money actually is exactly what's used to pay for things, like trading $1 for an apple.

slides.title: Where does money come from?
slides.text: Grown-ups usually earn money by doing work. For example, a teacher is paid for teaching and a driver is paid for driving. Kids may earn a little money or points by helping with agreed-upon chores.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teacher gets paid for teaching at school. Why does she receive money?

options.label: She's paid for doing work
options.outcome: Exactly right! Grown-ups usually earn money by doing work, like a teacher being paid for teaching.

options.label: Money just appears for no reason
options.outcome: Money doesn't just appear — it's usually earned by doing work, like teaching.

options.label: Only kids can receive money, not adults
options.outcome: Adults earn money too, usually by working — like a teacher being paid for teaching.

slides.title: How can chores help you earn?
slides.text: A chore is a helpful job at home, such as feeding a pet or putting away laundry. Sometimes families give money or points for certain extra chores. You do the job first, then earn the reward.

widgetConfig.scenario: A family gives money for an extra chore, like feeding a pet. When do you earn the reward?

options.label: After you do the job
options.outcome: Exactly right! You do the job first, then earn the reward.

options.label: Before doing any work at all
options.outcome: You earn the reward after doing the job, not before any work is done.

options.label: Chores never connect to earning money
options.outcome: Chores actually can connect to earning money, especially for extra jobs families choose to reward.

slides.title: Why can some chores earn more?
slides.text: Some jobs take more time or effort than others. Putting away five toys is quick, but helping clean a whole room takes longer. A bigger job may earn a bigger reward.

widgetConfig.scenario: Cleaning your whole room pays more points than putting away one toy. Why do you think that is?

options.label: Bigger or harder chores usually earn more
options.outcome: Exactly right! The amount of effort and time a chore takes usually affects how much it's worth.

options.label: All chores should pay the exact same no matter what
options.outcome: Actually, chores that take more time or effort usually earn more — that's fair since more work is being done.

options.label: It's totally random with no reason
options.outcome: There's usually a real reason — bigger or harder chores take more effort, so they're often worth more.

slides.title: What is an allowance?
slides.text: An allowance is a small amount of money some kids receive regularly, such as every week. It gives you a chance to practice choosing: spend some now, save some for later, or share some.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your parents give you a small amount of money each week for doing chores. What is this called?

options.label: An allowance
options.outcome: Exactly right! An allowance is regular money you might get, often for helping with chores.

options.label: A loan you have to pay back
options.outcome: An allowance isn't a loan — you don't have to pay it back, it's given to you regularly.

options.label: Free money with no reason
options.outcome: An allowance is usually tied to chores or responsibilities, not just free money for no reason.

slides.title: Why should you count your money?
slides.text: Counting tells you exactly how much money you have. If you have four $1 bills, you have $4. Then you can check whether you have enough for something you want.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have four $1 bills. Why is counting them useful?

options.label: It tells you exactly how much you have
options.outcome: Exactly right! Counting tells you exactly how much money you have, so you can check if you have enough for something.

options.label: Counting money never tells you anything useful
options.outcome: Counting money actually tells you a lot — exactly how much you have to spend.

options.label: Guessing is just as good as counting
options.outcome: Guessing isn't as reliable as counting — counting tells you the exact amount you have.

slides.title: Why does earned money feel special?
slides.text: When you earn money by helping, you can remember the work you did to get it. If you earned $3 by helping wash the car, spending or saving that $3 can feel extra meaningful.

widgetConfig.scenario: You earned $5 by helping with chores, versus being given $5. Why might the earned money feel more special?

options.label: You remember the work you did to get it
options.outcome: Exactly right! Earned money feels special because you remember the effort behind it.

options.label: It's actually worth more money
options.outcome: The dollar amount is the same — what's different is the memory of the effort you put in to earn it.

options.label: There's no difference at all
options.outcome: There is a difference in how it feels — earned money carries the memory of the work behind it, even though the amount is the same.

slides.title: Where should you keep your money?
slides.text: Money is easier to use when you keep it somewhere safe. Coins can go in a piggy bank and bills can go in a wallet or money jar. A safe spot helps you avoid losing what you worked for.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to avoid losing your coins and bills. What helps?

options.label: Keep it somewhere safe, like a piggy bank or wallet
options.outcome: Exactly right! A safe spot, like a piggy bank or wallet, helps you avoid losing what you worked for.

options.label: Leave it scattered anywhere
options.outcome: Leaving money scattered makes it easy to lose — a safe spot like a piggy bank protects it better.

options.label: Where you keep money never matters
options.outcome: Where you keep money actually matters — a safe spot helps you avoid losing it.

quiz.question: What is money used for?
choices: Buying things you need or want
It has no real use
quiz.explanation: Money buys things like food and toys. You give money, and you get a snack.

quiz.question: Where does most money come from?
choices: Work, like a job or chores
It just appears with no reason
quiz.explanation: Most money comes from work. A grown-up goes to a job, and kids can earn some doing chores.

quiz.question: What is a chore?
choices: A job you do, like sweeping or feeding a pet
A kind of candy
quiz.explanation: A chore is a job at home, like sweeping the floor. Doing chores can earn you money.

quiz.question: Which chore would likely pay more?
choices: Cleaning a whole room
Putting away one toy
quiz.explanation: Bigger jobs take more work, so they pay more. Cleaning a whole room earns more than putting away one toy.

quiz.question: What is an allowance?
choices: A little money you get regularly
A type of toy
quiz.explanation: An allowance is money you get regularly, like every Friday. It might be a few coins each week.

quiz.question: Why count your money?
choices: To know how much you have
Counting money is not useful
quiz.explanation: Counting your coins shows how much you have. Then you know if you can buy a $1 sticker.

quiz.question: Why can earned money feel extra special?
choices: Because you worked hard for it
Earned money feels just like any other money
quiz.explanation: You worked hard to earn it, like raking leaves. That hard work can make the money feel extra special.

quiz.question: Where is a safe place to keep your money?
choices: A piggy bank or a wallet
Anywhere on the floor
quiz.explanation: A piggy bank or wallet keeps coins from getting lost. Then your money stays safe until you need it.

quiz.question: Why is it good to keep your money safe?
choices: So you don't lose it before you can use it
Because money is not important
quiz.explanation: Safe money doesn't get lost or dropped. Then it's still there when you want to buy something.

quiz.question: What can you do before you spend your allowance?
choices: Count it to see how much you have
Just guess and hope it's enough
quiz.explanation: Count your coins first. Then you'll know if you have enough for the toy you want.

slides.title: What is the difference between a need and a want?
slides.text: A need is something important for living and staying healthy, like food, water, or a warm coat. A want is something fun or nice to have, like a new toy. We can enjoy wants, but needs usually come first.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap a button for each one

slides.title: What does it mean to save money?
slides.text: Saving means keeping some money for later instead of spending it right away. If you get $2 and put $1 in your piggy bank, you are saving. Little amounts can grow when you keep adding to them.

widgetConfig.scenario: Instead of spending all your money right away, you put some aside for later. What is this called?

options.label: Saving
options.outcome: Exactly right! Saving means keeping some money aside instead of spending it all right away.

options.label: Wasting money
options.outcome: Saving isn't wasting — it's setting money aside so you have it for later.

options.label: Losing money
options.outcome: Saved money isn't lost — it's still yours, just set aside for something later.

slides.title: What if you don't have enough money yet?
slides.text: You do not always have to buy something right away. If a toy costs $6 and you have $3, you can keep saving until you reach $6. Waiting can help you get something you really want.

widgetConfig.scenario: A toy costs $6, but you only have $4. What can you do?

options.label: Wait and save a little more until you have enough
options.outcome: Exactly right! You do not always have to buy something right away — waiting and saving a little more works well.

options.label: Take the toy anyway without paying
options.outcome: Taking something without paying isn't right — saving a little more until you have enough is the correct approach.

options.label: Give up on ever getting the toy
options.outcome: You don't have to give up — saving a bit more until you reach $6 will get you there.

slides.title: Why can't we buy everything we want?
slides.text: Money is limited, so choosing one thing can mean waiting for another. If you have $5, you might choose a book or a small toy, but not both. Making choices is part of using money.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $5 and want both a book and a toy. What's true about money?

options.label: Money is limited, so you may have to choose
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money is limited, so choosing one thing can mean waiting for another — making choices is part of using money.

options.label: Money never runs out, so you can buy everything
options.outcome: Money actually is limited — that's exactly why choosing between a book and a toy might be necessary.

options.label: Choosing isn't part of using money
options.outcome: Choosing is actually a big part of using money, especially when you can't buy everything you want.

slides.title: Why should you compare prices?
slides.text: The same thing can cost different amounts in different places. If one store sells a ball for $6 and another sells it for $5, the $5 ball leaves you $1 to save. Checking prices can help your money go further.

widgetConfig.scenario: A ball costs $6 at one store and $5 at another. Why check prices first?

options.label: The cheaper price leaves you more money to save
options.outcome: Exactly right! Checking prices first means the $5 ball leaves you $1 to save, instead of spending more than you need to.

options.label: Prices are always exactly the same everywhere
options.outcome: Prices actually can differ between stores — checking first can save you money.

options.label: Comparing prices never helps your money go further
options.outcome: Comparing prices actually helps a lot — it can leave you with extra money to save.

slides.title: How can money be used to help others?
slides.text: Money is not only for buying things for yourself. You might use some to buy a birthday card, donate to an animal shelter, or help someone in need. Giving is one way money can show kindness.

widgetConfig.scenario: Is money only for buying things for yourself?

options.label: No — you can also use it to help others, like donating
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money is not only for buying things for yourself — you can donate or help someone in need too.

options.label: Yes, money can only ever be spent on yourself
options.outcome: Money isn't only for yourself — you can use it to help others too, like donating to a shelter.

options.label: Giving money away never shows kindness
options.outcome: Giving money away actually is a way to show kindness, like helping someone in need.

slides.title: How do you choose what to buy?
slides.text: Sometimes you have enough money for only one thing. You can stop, look at your choices, and pick the one you care about most. Choosing on purpose is smarter than grabbing the first thing you see.

widgetConfig.scenario: You only have enough money for one thing. What's smarter than grabbing the first item you see?

options.label: Look at your choices and pick what you care about most
options.outcome: Exactly right! Stopping to look at your choices and picking what you care about most is smarter than grabbing the first thing you see.

options.label: Grab the very first thing you see
options.outcome: Grabbing the first thing you see skips thinking about what you actually care about most — looking at your choices works better.

options.label: Choosing on purpose never matters
options.outcome: Choosing on purpose actually matters a lot — it helps you pick what you truly care about.

slides.title: Would you rather buy a small treat or save for something bigger?
slides.text: A small treat may be fun right now, while a bigger item may take more saving. For example, you could spend $1 on candy today or save several dollars toward a toy. Neither choice is always right—the important part is choosing on purpose.

widgetConfig.scenario: Is a small treat now always the wrong choice compared to saving for something bigger?

options.label: No — neither choice is always right, as long as it is on purpose
options.outcome: Exactly right! Neither choice is always right — the important part is choosing on purpose, whether it's a treat now or saving for later.

options.label: Yes, saving is always the only right choice
options.outcome: Saving isn't always the only right choice — a small treat can be a fine choice too, as long as it's made on purpose.

options.label: Small treats are always a waste of money
options.outcome: Small treats aren't always a waste — the important part is choosing on purpose, not which option you pick.

slides.title: What should you ask before buying something?
slides.text: Ask yourself, “Do I need this, or do I just want it?” Then ask, “Do I still want it enough to spend my money on it?” Those two questions can help you make a thoughtful choice.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to buy something. What question helps you decide thoughtfully?

options.label: "Do I need this, or do I just want it?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Asking yourself this question, and whether you still want it enough to spend your money, helps you make a thoughtful choice.

options.label: Nothing — just buy it with no questions
options.outcome: Buying with no questions at all skips a helpful step — asking yourself a thoughtful question first helps you decide.

options.label: Asking questions before buying never helps
options.outcome: Asking questions before buying actually helps a lot — it leads to a more thoughtful choice.

quiz.question: Which one is a need, not a want?
choices: Food to eat
A new toy
quiz.explanation: A need is something your body must have, like food. A toy is nice, but it's a want.

quiz.question: What does saving money mean?
choices: Keeping money instead of spending it right away
Spending every coin the moment you get it
quiz.explanation: Saving means keeping your coins instead of spending them. You put coins in a piggy bank to save them.

quiz.question: What can help if a toy costs more than you have?
choices: Waiting and saving a little more
Giving up on ever getting it
quiz.explanation: You can wait and save more coins. Adding a coin each week can get you to the toy.

quiz.question: Why can't you buy everything you want?
choices: You only have a limited amount of money
Money never runs out
quiz.explanation: You only have so many coins. Buying a toy today means waiting to buy the candy tomorrow.

quiz.question: Why check prices at two different stores?
choices: The same toy can cost less somewhere else
Prices are always exactly the same everywhere
quiz.explanation: The same toy can cost less at another store. Checking first can save you coins to spend later.

quiz.question: What is one kind way to use money?
choices: Giving a gift to someone you love
Never sharing it with anyone
quiz.explanation: You can buy a gift for someone you love. Giving a friend a small present shows you care.

quiz.question: At the store, why might you pick just one thing?
choices: You might only have enough money for one
Stores only allow one item per visit
quiz.explanation: You might only have enough coins for one item. So you pick your favorite, like a red balloon.

quiz.question: What is true about a small treat?
choices: It costs a little and is gone fast
It always costs more than a toy
quiz.explanation: A small treat, like a candy, costs a little. But it is eaten fast and then it's gone.

quiz.question: What should you ask before buying something?
choices: Do I need it, or do I just want it?
How fast can I buy it?
quiz.explanation: Ask yourself: do I need this, or do I just want it? A snack you need matters more than a want.

quiz.question: Why is picking a bigger toy over a small treat sometimes a good choice?
choices: The toy can last a long time
The toy always costs less
quiz.explanation: A bigger toy costs more coins, but you can play with it for a long time, not just one bite.

slides.title: What is an allowance?
slides.text: An allowance is money some kids receive regularly, such as once a week. Sometimes it is connected to chores and sometimes it is simply for learning money skills. If you receive $10, you get to practice deciding how much to spend, save, or give.

widgetConfig.scenario: You receive $10 regularly as an allowance. What does this let you practice?

options.label: Deciding how much to spend, save, or give
options.outcome: Exactly right! An allowance lets you practice deciding how much to spend, save, or give.

options.label: Nothing — allowances teach no money skills
options.outcome: Allowances actually teach real money skills, like practicing how much to spend, save, or give.

options.label: Allowances are always exactly tied to chores
options.outcome: An allowance isn't always tied to chores — sometimes it's simply for learning money skills.

slides.title: What is a simple budget?
slides.text: A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it. If you get 20 points this week, you might plan 10 for saving, 8 for spending, and 2 for giving. A plan helps you avoid wondering where all your money went.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get 20 points and want to plan how to use them before spending any. What is this plan called?

options.label: A budget
options.outcome: Exactly right! A budget is a plan for your money before you spend it.

options.label: A receipt
options.outcome: A receipt just records what you already spent — a plan made before spending is called a budget.

options.label: There is no way to plan money ahead of time
options.outcome: There actually is a way — making a budget is exactly how you plan your money before spending it.

slides.title: Why can different chores have different rewards?
slides.text: Jobs can take different amounts of time, effort, or skill. Wiping the table may take five minutes, while organizing the garage may take an hour. It makes sense for the harder job to be worth more.

widgetConfig.scenario: Wiping a table takes 5 minutes, but organizing a garage takes an hour. Why might they pay differently?

options.label: Jobs take different amounts of time, effort, or skill
options.outcome: Exactly right! Jobs can take different amounts of time, effort, or skill, so it makes sense for the harder job to be worth more.

options.label: All chores should pay exactly the same no matter what
options.outcome: Chores don't need to pay exactly the same — harder, longer jobs can reasonably be worth more.

options.label: Chore rewards never depend on effort
options.outcome: Chore rewards actually can depend on effort — jobs that take more time or skill can be worth more.

slides.title: How can you split your money three ways?
slides.text: A simple method is to divide money into spend, save, and give. For example, from $12 you might spend $5, save $5, and give $2. This lets you enjoy some now while preparing for later and helping others.

slides.title: Why should you track your money?
slides.text: Writing down what comes in and what goes out shows you what is really happening with your money. You may think you saved $10, but your list might show that small snacks used $4. Tracking replaces guessing with facts.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're not sure where your allowance goes each week. What would help you figure it out?

options.label: Write down what you earn and spend
options.outcome: Exactly! Tracking your money helps you see where it actually goes, so you can make better choices.

options.label: Just guess and hope for the best
options.outcome: Guessing won't show you the real picture — writing it down helps you actually understand your spending.

options.label: It doesn't matter where money goes
options.outcome: It actually does matter — tracking helps you notice patterns and make smarter choices with your money.

slides.title: How do you set a savings goal?
slides.text: Choose something specific, find its price, and decide how much you can save each week. If a game costs $40 and you save $10 a week, you can reach the goal in four weeks. A clear target makes saving easier to stick with.

widgetConfig.scenario: A game costs $40 and you save $10 a week. What makes this goal easier to stick with?

options.label: Choosing something specific with a clear price and plan
options.outcome: Exactly right! Choosing something specific, finding its price, and deciding how much to save each week makes a goal easier to stick with.

options.label: Having no specific target at all
options.outcome: Having no specific target makes saving harder to stick with — a clear goal and plan work much better.

options.label: Clear targets never help with saving
options.outcome: Clear targets actually help a lot with saving — they make the goal easier to stick with.

slides.title: What is bonus pay?
slides.text: Bonus pay is an extra reward for going beyond the basic job. For example, if you were asked to rake leaves and also neatly bagged them without being reminded, your family might choose to add a bonus. The key is agreeing on the rules ahead of time.

widgetConfig.scenario: You rake leaves and also neatly bag them without being asked. What might your family give you for the extra effort?

options.label: Bonus pay, agreed on ahead of time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Bonus pay is an extra reward for going beyond the basic job, with the rules agreed on ahead of time.

options.label: Nothing extra, no matter how much more you do
options.outcome: Going beyond the basic job can actually earn bonus pay, when the rules are agreed on ahead of time.

options.label: Bonus pay is decided only after the work with no agreement
options.outcome: The key to bonus pay is agreeing on the rules ahead of time, not deciding only afterward.

slides.title: Why plan your money for the whole week?
slides.text: If you spend everything on Monday, you may have nothing left when you want something on Saturday. Thinking about the whole week helps you decide how much to use now and how much to keep for later.

widgetConfig.scenario: You spend everything on Monday. What happens if you want something on Saturday?

options.label: You may have nothing left
options.outcome: Exactly right! If you spend everything on Monday, you may have nothing left when you want something on Saturday.

options.label: You will always have plenty left no matter what
options.outcome: Spending everything early can leave you with nothing left later — planning for the whole week helps avoid that.

options.label: Planning for the week never affects what is left later
options.outcome: Planning for the whole week actually affects this a lot — it helps you have money left when you need it.

slides.title: Why start with a small savings goal?
slides.text: Small goals give you practice and quick wins. Saving 5 points a week for a 20-point reward teaches the same habit you will use someday for much bigger goals. Big money habits often start small.

widgetConfig.scenario: You save 5 points a week for a 20-point reward. What does this small goal teach you?

options.label: The same habit you'll use for bigger goals someday
options.outcome: Exactly right! Small goals give you practice and quick wins — the same habit you'll use someday for much bigger goals.

options.label: Nothing useful, since the goal is too small
options.outcome: A small goal actually teaches something very useful — the same saving habit you'll use for bigger goals later.

options.label: Small goals never lead to good money habits
options.outcome: Small goals actually do lead to good money habits — big habits often start small.

A place to keep candy

Yes, every chore pays exactly the same

quiz.question: What is bonus pay?

Money you never actually receive

Small goals are pointless to set
