quiz.question: What usually determines how much a chore is worth?
choices: How much time and effort it takes
The color of the chore chart
quiz.explanation: A chore's pay usually depends on how much time and effort it takes. Vacuuming the whole house takes longer than wiping one counter, so it earns more.

slides.title: Why should you compare prices?
slides.text: Two stores can charge different prices for the exact same item. If a game is $25 in one place and $20 in another, comparing first saves $5. That $5 can stay in your savings or pay for something else later.

widgetConfig.scenario: A game is $25 in one place and $20 in another. What does comparing prices first save you?

options.label: $5 that can go to savings or something else
options.outcome: Exactly right! Comparing first saves $5, which can stay in your savings or pay for something else later.

options.label: Nothing — comparing prices never saves money
options.outcome: Comparing prices actually can save real money, like the $5 difference between two stores.

options.label: Prices are always identical everywhere
options.outcome: Prices actually can differ a lot between stores — comparing first can reveal real savings.

slides.title: What is a tradeoff?
slides.text: A tradeoff happens when choosing one thing means giving up another. If you have $20, you might choose a movie ticket or a toy, but not both today. The thing you do not choose is part of the tradeoff.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $10. You can buy a toy OR save it for a bigger toy later, not both. What is this choice called?

options.label: A tradeoff — choosing one option means giving up the other
options.outcome: Exactly! A tradeoff means choosing one thing means you give up the other option, at least for now.

options.label: A mistake no matter what you pick
options.outcome: It's not a mistake — tradeoffs are just a normal part of making choices with limited money.

options.label: Something that only happens with big purchases
options.outcome: Tradeoffs happen with purchases big and small — any time choosing one option means giving up another.

slides.title: What does borrowing mean?
slides.text: Borrowing means using money that belongs to someone else and promising to pay it back. If your sibling lends you $5, that $5 is not free—you now owe $5. Agreeing on when you will repay it keeps things fair.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your sibling lends you $5. Is this money free to keep?

options.label: No — you now owe $5 and should agree on repayment
options.outcome: Exactly right! Borrowing means using money that belongs to someone else and promising to pay it back — that $5 is not free.

options.label: Yes, borrowed money is always free
options.outcome: Borrowed money isn't free — you owe it back, and agreeing on repayment keeps things fair.

options.label: Borrowing never requires paying anything back
options.outcome: Borrowing actually always involves paying it back — that's the whole idea of borrowing versus receiving a gift.

slides.title: What can happen when you spend too fast?
slides.text: Spending everything right away can leave you stuck later. If you use all 20 points on Monday and a reward you really love appears on Friday, you cannot get it unless you earn or save more. Slowing down gives future-you more choices.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get $10 and spend it all on candy the same day. A week later, you really want to buy a toy but have no money left. What happened?

options.label: Spending it all right away meant nothing was left for something you wanted more later
options.outcome: Exactly — spending fast feels fun in the moment, but it can mean missing out on something you'd want even more later.

options.label: Nothing — spending money fast has no downside
options.outcome: Spending it all fast meant there was nothing left for the toy you wanted later — that's a real downside of spending too quickly.

options.label: The toy store should have given it to you anyway
options.outcome: The real lesson here is about planning — spending slower leaves room for things you want later.

slides.title: Why might you choose to give some money away?
slides.text: Giving lets your money help someone else. You might donate part of your allowance to a food drive or animal shelter. Even a small amount can matter when many people contribute.

widgetConfig.scenario: You donate part of your allowance to a food drive. What does giving let your money do?

options.label: Help someone else
options.outcome: Exactly right! Giving lets your money help someone else, even a small amount can matter when many people contribute.

options.label: Nothing — giving money away never helps anyone
options.outcome: Giving money away actually can help a lot, even in small amounts when many people contribute.

options.label: Only large amounts of money can ever help others
options.outcome: Even a small donated amount can matter, especially when many people contribute together.

slides.title: Why do prices change over time?
slides.text: Prices do not stay exactly the same forever. A snack that cost $2 before might cost $2.25 later because the costs of making and selling things can change. This is one reason money choices can look different over time.

widgetConfig.scenario: A snack that cost $2 before now costs $2.25. Why might this happen?

options.label: The costs of making and selling things can change
options.outcome: Exactly right! Prices do not stay exactly the same forever, because the costs of making and selling things can change over time.

options.label: Prices never change for any reason
options.outcome: Prices actually do change over time, because the costs of making and selling things can shift.

options.label: Only you control whether prices change
options.outcome: You don't control prices — they change because of shifting costs of making and selling things.

slides.title: Can a bigger pack sometimes be a better deal?
slides.text: Yes, because the total price is not the only number that matters. A 10-pack for $5 costs 50 cents each, while a 4-pack for $3 costs 75 cents each. The bigger pack is a better deal only if you will actually use it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A 10-pack costs $5 and a 5-pack costs $3. Which is the better deal per item?

options.label: The 10-pack — it costs less per item
options.outcome: Exactly! The 10-pack works out to 50 cents per item, cheaper than the 5-pack's 60 cents per item.

options.label: The 5-pack, since it costs less total
options.outcome: Looking at total price alone can be misleading — comparing the price per item shows the 10-pack is actually the better deal.

options.label: They're exactly the same deal
options.outcome: They're not the same — comparing price per item shows the 10-pack is the better value.

slides.title: What does it mean to split a cost?
slides.text: Splitting a cost means two or more people each pay part of the total. If a shared craft kit costs $20, two friends might each pay $10. Before splitting, agree on who owns it and how it will be shared.

widgetConfig.scenario: A shared craft kit costs $20, and two friends split it. How much might each pay?

options.label: $10 each, after agreeing on ownership and sharing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Splitting a cost means two or more people each pay part of the total, after agreeing on how it will be shared.

options.label: One person pays the full $20 alone
options.outcome: Splitting the cost means both people pay part of it, not just one person paying the whole $20 alone.

options.label: Splitting a cost never requires any agreement first
options.outcome: Splitting a cost actually requires agreeing first on ownership and how it'll be shared.

slides.title: Why pause before a big purchase?
slides.text: Big purchases can use up a lot of your money at once. Waiting a little gives you time to ask, “Do I still want this?” and “What will I give up if I buy it?” A short pause can prevent a decision you regret.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to make a big purchase. What can a short pause help you do?

options.label: Ask if you still want it and what you would give up
options.outcome: Exactly right! A short pause gives you time to ask 'Do I still want this?' and 'What will I give up if I buy it?', which can prevent a decision you regret.

options.label: Nothing — pausing before a big purchase never helps
options.outcome: Pausing before a big purchase actually helps a lot — it can prevent a decision you'd later regret.

options.label: Big purchases should always happen immediately with no thought
options.outcome: Big purchases benefit from a pause to think it through, rather than happening immediately with no thought.

quiz.question: Why compare prices before buying?
choices: The same item can cost different amounts in different places
Prices are always exactly the same everywhere
quiz.explanation: The exact same toy can be cheaper at one store than another. Checking prices first, before you buy, helps your points go further.

quiz.question: What is a tradeoff?
choices: Choosing one want over another because you can't have both
Getting two things at once for free
quiz.explanation: A tradeoff is picking one want over another because you can't have both. If you have 20 points, choosing a toy means the movie ticket has to wait.

quiz.question: What does borrowing money mean?
choices: Using someone else's money now and paying it back later
Money that never has to be paid back
quiz.explanation: Borrowing means using someone else's money now and promising to pay it back later. Agreeing on when you'll repay a sibling keeps things fair between you.

quiz.question: What can happen if you spend all your money right away?
choices: You might have nothing left when something better comes along
Nothing — spending fast has no downside
quiz.explanation: Spending every point the day you get it can feel fun in the moment. But then you might have nothing left when something better comes along.

quiz.question: Why might you give some of your money away?
choices: It can help others and feels good
Money should never be shared with anyone
quiz.explanation: Giving a few points to a friend in need can help them and feel good to you too. It also builds a caring habit that lasts.

quiz.question: Why do prices sometimes go up over time?
choices: The cost of things doesn't always stay the same
Prices are locked forever and never change
quiz.explanation: Prices don't always stay the same as time passes. A snack that cost 5 points last year might cost 6 points now.

quiz.question: Why might a bigger bag of chips be a smarter buy?
choices: It can cost less for each chip inside
Big bags are always more expensive per chip
quiz.explanation: A big bag costs more overall, but each chip inside can cost less than in a small bag. Checking the size helps you spend smarter.

quiz.question: What does it mean to split a cost with a friend?
choices: Each person pays part of the price
One person pays for everything
quiz.explanation: Splitting a cost means two people each pay part of the price. If a toy costs 20 points, you and a friend might each pay 10.

quiz.question: Why pause before a big purchase?
choices: It gives you time to think it over
Pausing always makes things more expensive
quiz.explanation: Taking a breath before spending a lot of points gives you time to think it over. That short pause can stop a choice you might regret.

quiz.question: If a toy costs more than your allowance this week, what's a smart choice?
choices: Wait, save more, or split the cost with someone
Buy it anyway even without enough money
quiz.explanation: You could wait and save more, or split the cost with a friend. Both are smarter than buying it without having enough.

slides.title: What is the difference between price and value?
slides.text: Price is the amount something costs; value is how useful or meaningful it is to you. A $6 book you read five times may give you more value than a $25 gadget you stop using after one day. The highest price does not always mean the highest value.

widgetConfig.scenario: A $6 book you read five times versus a $25 gadget you stop using after one day. Which gives more value?

options.label: The $6 book, despite its lower price
options.outcome: Exactly right! Value is how useful or meaningful something is to you — the highest price does not always mean the highest value.

options.label: The $25 gadget, since it costs more
options.outcome: A higher price doesn't automatically mean higher value — the $6 book used five times can be worth more to you.

options.label: Price and value always mean exactly the same thing
options.outcome: Price and value aren't the same thing — something cheaper can actually give you more value.

slides.title: How can cost per unit reveal the better deal?
slides.text: Cost per unit tells you what each item, ounce, or piece really costs. A 10-pack of pencils for $2 costs 20 cents per pencil, while a 4-pack for $1 costs 25 cents each. Comparing units helps you look past the bigger price tag.

widgetConfig.scenario: One bag of 10 apples costs $5, another bag of 4 apples costs $3. Which tells you the real better deal?

options.label: Comparing the cost per apple in each bag
options.outcome: Exactly! Cost per unit tells you what each item really costs, which reveals the better deal more clearly than total price alone.

options.label: Just looking at the total price of each bag
options.outcome: Total price alone can be misleading — comparing cost per item reveals which bag is actually the better deal.

options.label: Whichever bag has a bigger picture on it
options.outcome: The picture on the bag has nothing to do with value — comparing cost per apple is what actually reveals the better deal.

slides.title: Does a sale sign always mean a good deal?
slides.text: No. A discount only matters compared with the normal price and other available prices. If an item is marked “30% off” but another store sells the same item for less, the flashy sale is not the best deal. Compare before assuming.

widgetConfig.scenario: A store has a big "SALE!" sign on an item, but you realize the "sale price" is actually the same as what other stores normally charge. Is it really a deal?

options.label: No — a sale sign doesn't automatically mean it's cheaper than elsewhere
options.outcome: Exactly right — marketing can make something look like a deal even when it isn't. It's worth comparing the actual price, not just trusting the sign.

options.label: Yes, sale signs always mean real savings
options.outcome: Not always — some 'sale' prices are the same as (or barely below) normal prices elsewhere. It's worth comparing before assuming it's a deal.

options.label: It doesn't matter, sales are always fake
options.outcome: Some sales are genuinely good deals — the key is checking the actual price elsewhere rather than assuming either way.

slides.title: Why should you read the fine print?
slides.text: The headline price may not tell the whole story. Shipping fees, service charges, return limits, or membership rules can change the real cost. A $15 item with $8 shipping actually costs $23, so details matter.

widgetConfig.scenario: A $15 item has $8 shipping. What's the real cost?

options.label: $23, once shipping is included
options.outcome: Exactly right! The headline price may not tell the whole story — a $15 item with $8 shipping actually costs $23.

options.label: $15, since shipping never counts
options.outcome: Shipping actually does count toward the real cost — the true total here is $23, not just $15.

options.label: The fine print never changes the real cost of anything
options.outcome: The fine print actually can change the real cost quite a bit, like extra shipping fees.

slides.title: Is a name brand always better than a store brand?
slides.text: Not necessarily. Store brands often offer a similar product for less because you are not paying as much for the brand name or marketing. Comparing ingredients, features, or quality can tell you whether the extra price is worth it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A name-brand cereal costs $5 and a store-brand version with similar ingredients costs $3. What's the smart choice?

options.label: Compare the actual ingredients/quality, not just the brand name
options.outcome: Exactly — brand names often cost more due to marketing, not necessarily better quality. Comparing the actual product helps you decide if it's worth the extra cost.

options.label: Always buy the name brand since it must be better
options.outcome: Name brands aren't automatically better — sometimes you're mostly paying extra for marketing, not quality.

options.label: Always buy the store brand no matter what
options.outcome: Store brands aren't automatically better either — the smart move is comparing the actual product, not assuming based on price alone.

slides.title: When is buying in bulk actually smart?
slides.text: Buying more at once can lower the cost per item, but only if you will use everything. Saving $5 on a giant snack box is not a deal if half goes stale. A good bulk purchase saves money without creating waste.

widgetConfig.scenario: You save $5 on a giant snack box, but half of it goes stale before you finish. Was this a good deal?

options.label: Not really — a good bulk purchase shouldn't create waste
options.outcome: Exactly right! Buying more at once can lower the cost per item, but only if you'll use everything — saving $5 isn't a deal if half goes stale.

options.label: Yes, bulk buying is always a smart deal no matter what
options.outcome: Bulk buying isn't always smart — if a lot goes to waste, the savings don't really pay off.

options.label: Buying in bulk never has any downside
options.outcome: Buying in bulk actually can have a real downside, like wasted food that goes stale before you use it.

slides.title: Why should you check a receipt?
slides.text: A receipt is a record of what you bought and what you were charged. Checking it can catch mistakes such as being charged twice or getting the wrong price. It also helps you see exactly where your money went.

widgetConfig.scenario: You might have been charged twice by mistake. What helps you catch this?

options.label: Checking your receipt
options.outcome: Exactly right! A receipt is a record of what you bought and what you were charged — checking it can catch mistakes like being charged twice.

options.label: Never checking receipts at all
options.outcome: Never checking receipts means mistakes like double charges could go unnoticed — checking catches them.

options.label: Receipts never reveal any mistakes
options.outcome: Receipts actually can reveal real mistakes, like being charged twice or getting the wrong price.

slides.title: What extra fees can change the real price?
slides.text: Shipping, service, delivery, processing, and convenience fees can all make a purchase cost more than the advertised price. A $20 ticket with $7 in fees really costs $27. Always compare the final total, not just the first number you see.

widgetConfig.scenario: A $20 ticket has $7 in fees. What's the real total cost?

options.label: $27, once fees are included
options.outcome: Exactly right! Shipping, service, and other fees can all make a purchase cost more than the advertised price — this ticket really costs $27.

options.label: $20, since fees never count toward the real price
options.outcome: Fees actually do count toward the real price — this ticket's true cost is $27, not just $20.

options.label: Extra fees never change what you actually pay
options.outcome: Extra fees actually can change what you pay quite a bit — always compare the final total, not just the first number.

slides.title: Why do return policies matter?
slides.text: A return policy tells you what happens if an item does not fit, breaks, or is not what you expected. A cheaper item with “no returns” may be riskier than a slightly more expensive one you can return. Policies are part of the deal.

widgetConfig.scenario: A cheaper item has 'no returns.' Is this automatically a better deal than a pricier item you can return?

options.label: Not necessarily — "no returns" can make it riskier
options.outcome: Exactly right! A cheaper item with 'no returns' may be riskier than a slightly more expensive one you can return — policies are part of the deal.

options.label: Yes, cheaper is always better no matter the return policy
options.outcome: Cheaper isn't always better — a 'no returns' policy adds real risk that's worth weighing against the price.

options.label: Return policies never matter when buying something
options.outcome: Return policies actually matter a lot — they tell you what happens if an item doesn't work out.

quiz.question: What's the difference between price and value?
choices: Price is the cost, value is how much it's worth to you
They always mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: Price is simply the number on the tag, but value is how much something is actually worth to you personally. A $5 book you'll read many times might be worth more than a $20 toy you play with once.

quiz.question: What does comparing the price per unit help you find?
choices: Which option is actually the better deal
It never matters what size you buy
quiz.explanation: Comparing price per unit means dividing the total cost by how many items or ounces you get. A 10-pack of pencils for $2 costs less per pencil than a 4-pack for $1, even though the 4-pack's tag looks smaller.

quiz.question: Why isn't every discount a real deal?
choices: Some prices are raised before being marked down
Sale prices are always the lowest possible price
quiz.explanation: Some stores raise a price right before marking it 'on sale,' making the discount look bigger than it really is. A $30 item raised from $20 and then marked down to $25 isn't actually a bargain, even with a big sign.

quiz.question: Why check the fine print before a purchase?
choices: Hidden costs like fees can make a deal less good than it looks
The fine print never matters
quiz.explanation: A good-looking deal can hide extra costs, like a shipping fee or a short return window. A toy that looks cheap online might cost more once shipping is added, so checking the full price avoids a surprise.

quiz.question: Why might a store brand be a smart choice?
choices: It often costs less for a nearly identical product
Store brands are always lower quality
quiz.explanation: A store's own brand is often made very similarly to a famous name brand, but sold for less money. Trying the cheaper store brand first can save money without giving up much quality.

quiz.question: When is buying in bulk actually a good deal?
choices: Only if you'll use it all before it spoils or goes to waste
Buying in bulk is always the best choice no matter what
quiz.explanation: Buying a big pack usually lowers the price for each item inside it. But that only helps if you actually use everything before it spoils or gets old, like a giant bag of chips going stale.

quiz.question: Why check your receipt after a purchase?
choices: It can reveal a mistake or an unexpected charge
Receipts never contain useful information
quiz.explanation: A receipt lists every item and fee from your purchase, so checking it can catch a mistake, like being charged twice for one item. Comparing it to what you meant to buy is a smart habit.

quiz.question: What can make an item cost more than its listed price?
choices: Extra fees like shipping or service charges
Extra fees are illegal and never happen
quiz.explanation: Extra fees, like a shipping charge or a service fee, can get added on at checkout. A $10 item with a $5 shipping fee actually costs $15, so adding up the true total before buying avoids a surprise.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to know a store's return policy before buying?
choices: It protects you if the item turns out to be the wrong choice
Return policies never matter once you've paid
quiz.explanation: Knowing you can return or exchange an item protects you if it turns out to be the wrong size or doesn't work as expected. A generous return policy makes trying something new feel less risky.

quiz.question: What's a smart habit when comparing two similar products?
choices: Check the price per unit and read the fine print
Just grab whichever one is closest on the shelf
quiz.explanation: Checking the price per unit and reading the fine print both help you spot the real cost, not just what the tag says. Together, these habits help you find the option that's actually the better deal.

slides.title: What is opportunity cost?
slides.text: Opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose one option instead of another. If you spend $20 on snacks, you also give up the chance to put that $20 toward a game. Every choice uses money that could have been used somewhere else.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $20. You can either buy a video game now, or save it toward a $100 bike you really want. What's the opportunity cost of buying the game?

options.label: You're $20 further from being able to buy the bike
options.outcome: Exactly — opportunity cost is what you give up by choosing one thing over another. Spending the $20 now means it's no longer working toward the bike.

options.label: There is no real cost since you have the money
options.outcome: Even if you have the money, spending it on one thing means you can't spend it on something else — that trade-off is the opportunity cost.

options.label: The cost is exactly $100
options.outcome: The opportunity cost here is the $20 and its progress toward the bike, not the full $100 price of the bike.

slides.title: How can you avoid impulse buys?
slides.text: An impulse buy happens when excitement makes you purchase before thinking. Try a 24-hour rule for nonessential items: save the item, wait a day, then decide again. If you still want it and it fits your budget, the choice is more thoughtful.

widgetConfig.scenario: You see something exciting at the store and want to buy it immediately. What's a smart strategy to avoid regretting it?

options.label: Wait 24 hours before deciding to buy it
options.outcome: Great strategy! Waiting a day often helps you tell the difference between a real want and a passing impulse.

options.label: Always buy it immediately, no matter what
options.outcome: Buying immediately on impulse often leads to regret later — waiting a bit helps you decide more clearly.

options.label: Never buy anything you get excited about
options.outcome: You don't have to avoid everything exciting — just pausing briefly before buying helps you decide more wisely.

slides.title: Why divide a budget into categories?
slides.text: Categories give each part of your money a job. You might divide $30 into $15 saving, $10 spending, and $5 giving. This makes it easier to protect important goals instead of spending from one big pile.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have $30 to use over a month. Why might dividing it into categories, like food, fun, and savings, help?

options.label: It gives each part of your money a clear job
options.outcome: Exactly right! Categories give each part of your money a job, which helps you use it intentionally instead of randomly.

options.label: Dividing it into categories makes no difference
options.outcome: Dividing into categories actually helps a lot — it gives each part of your money a clear purpose.

options.label: You should spend it all on one category only
options.outcome: Spending it all on one category defeats the purpose — dividing it gives each need its own planned amount.

slides.title: How do people earn money by creating value?
slides.text: People are usually paid for solving problems or doing something useful. A teen who designs a poster, tutors a younger student, or mows a lawn is providing value to someone else. Skills that solve bigger problems can often earn more.

widgetConfig.scenario: A teen tutors a younger student or mows a lawn. What are they doing?

options.label: Providing value to someone else
options.outcome: Exactly right! People are usually paid for solving problems or doing something useful — this teen is providing real value to someone else.

options.label: Nothing — this never counts as earning money
options.outcome: This actually is a real way of earning money — providing a useful service to someone else.

options.label: Only adults can ever earn money this way
options.outcome: Teens can earn money this way too, by providing a useful skill or service, not just adults.

slides.title: Can time have an opportunity cost too?
slides.text: Yes. An hour spent on one activity cannot also be spent on another. Choosing two hours of gaming may mean giving up two hours you could have used for homework, practice, or paid work. Good decisions consider both time and money.

widgetConfig.scenario: You spend two hours gaming instead of doing homework. What did you give up?

options.label: The two hours you could have used for homework
options.outcome: Exactly right! An hour spent on one activity cannot also be spent on another — choosing gaming means giving up that time for homework or something else.

options.label: Nothing — time never has an opportunity cost
options.outcome: Time actually does have an opportunity cost — choosing one activity means giving up what you could have done instead.

options.label: Only money, never time, has an opportunity cost
options.outcome: Time also has an opportunity cost, just like money — choosing one activity means giving up another.

slides.title: Why can subscriptions become a money trap?
slides.text: Subscriptions feel small because the charge repeats a little at a time. But $8 every month becomes $96 in a year, even if you barely use the service. Reviewing subscriptions helps you stop paying for things you no longer value.

widgetConfig.scenario: A subscription costs $8 a month. How much does this add up to in a year?

options.label: $96, even if you barely use it
options.outcome: Exactly right! Subscriptions feel small because the charge repeats a little at a time, but $8 every month becomes $96 in a year.

options.label: Exactly $8 total for the whole year
options.outcome: It's not just $8 for the year — the monthly charge repeats, adding up to $96 over twelve months.

options.label: Subscriptions never add up to anything meaningful
options.outcome: Subscriptions actually can add up to a lot — small monthly charges become a big total over a year.

slides.title: How can a skill become income?
slides.text: A useful skill can sometimes become a small business or paid service. If you are good at drawing, tutoring, editing videos, or fixing bikes, someone may be willing to pay for that help. Start by asking what problem your skill can solve.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're good at drawing or fixing bikes. How might this become income?

options.label: Someone may pay for that skill as a service
options.outcome: Exactly right! A useful skill can sometimes become a small business or paid service — start by asking what problem your skill can solve.

options.label: Skills can never become a source of income
options.outcome: Skills actually can become a real source of income, as a small business or paid service.

options.label: Only certain approved skills can ever earn money
options.outcome: Many different skills, like drawing or fixing bikes, can become income if they solve a problem someone will pay for.

slides.title: Why agree on pay before doing a job?
slides.text: Clear expectations prevent arguments later. Before walking a dog or helping with yard work, agree on the job, the deadline, and the pay. Then both people know what “done” means and what the work is worth.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're about to walk a dog for pay. What helps prevent arguments later?

options.label: Agreeing on the job, deadline, and pay ahead of time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Clear expectations prevent arguments later — agreeing on the job, deadline, and pay beforehand means both people know what's expected.

options.label: Figuring out pay only after the work is done
options.outcome: Figuring out pay only afterward can lead to disagreements — agreeing ahead of time prevents that.

options.label: Agreeing on pay beforehand never prevents disagreements
options.outcome: Agreeing on pay beforehand actually does prevent disagreements, by making sure both people know what to expect.

slides.title: How can small purchases compete with a big goal?
slides.text: Small purchases can quietly add up. Spending $5 three times a week is about $60 in four weeks. Seeing the total helps you decide whether those small treats matter more to you than the bigger goal you are saving for.

widgetConfig.scenario: You spend $5 three times a week. How much does this add up to in four weeks?

options.label: About $60
options.outcome: Exactly right! Spending $5 three times a week is about $60 in four weeks — seeing the total helps you decide if it matters more than your bigger goal.

options.label: Exactly $5 total, no matter how often you spend it
options.outcome: It's not just $5 total — spending it repeatedly adds up to about $60 over four weeks.

options.label: Small purchases never add up to anything significant
options.outcome: Small purchases actually can add up to something significant, like $60 over just four weeks.

quiz.question: What is opportunity cost?
choices: What you give up by choosing to spend money one way instead of another
A type of coupon
quiz.explanation: Opportunity cost is what you give up when you choose to spend your money one way instead of another. Spending your whole allowance on snacks this week means giving up the chance to put that money toward a bigger goal.

quiz.question: What's a smart way to avoid impulse buys?
choices: Wait a day before deciding to buy something
Always buy the moment you see something you want
quiz.explanation: An impulse buy happens when you grab something the instant you see it, without thinking it through. Waiting even one day often reveals whether you truly wanted it or just got excited in the moment.

quiz.question: What does splitting money into categories like saving, spending, and giving do?
choices: Builds multiple good money habits at once
Makes budgeting impossible
quiz.explanation: Instead of treating your money as one big pile, splitting it into categories builds several good habits at once. Putting 15 points toward saving, 10 toward spending, and 5 toward giving practices all three skills together.

quiz.question: How do people usually earn money?
choices: By providing something useful or valuable to someone else
Money appears with no connection to effort
quiz.explanation: People are usually paid for doing something useful for someone else, and the more value they provide, the more they can earn. Mowing a neighbor's whole yard is worth more than picking up a few sticks, because it solves a bigger problem.

quiz.question: Is time a kind of opportunity cost too?
choices: Yes, choosing one activity means giving up another
No, only money can be an opportunity cost
quiz.explanation: Choosing to spend an hour playing a game means you can't spend that same hour doing homework or practicing a skill. Time works just like money — using it on one thing means giving up another.

quiz.question: Why review your subscriptions regularly?
choices: You might be paying for something you don't use anymore
Subscriptions always cancel themselves automatically
quiz.explanation: A subscription can keep charging your account every month even after you've stopped using it. Checking your subscriptions regularly stops you from quietly paying for something you don't actually want anymore.

quiz.question: What's one way to think about earning money from a skill?
choices: Consider turning something you're good at into paid work
Skills have nothing to do with earning money
quiz.explanation: A skill you're already good at, like drawing or fixing things, can sometimes be turned into paid work. Thinking about your existing skills can reveal earning opportunities you hadn't considered.

quiz.question: When is the best time to agree on pay for a job?
choices: Before you start the job
After you've already finished it
quiz.explanation: Agreeing on pay before you start a job, like walking a neighbor's dog, avoids confusion or disappointment afterward. It protects both you and the person hiring you.

quiz.question: What can happen if you spend a little often on small things?
choices: It can add up to more than a bigger purchase you'd value more
Small purchases never add up to anything
quiz.explanation: Buying a small treat almost every day can quietly add up to more money than one bigger purchase you'd actually value more. Comparing many small buys to a single big one can change how you decide to spend.

quiz.question: What do opportunity cost and budgeting into categories have in common?
choices: Both help you make thoughtful choices about limited money
They are unrelated ideas with nothing in common
quiz.explanation: Both ideas are tools for making thoughtful choices when your money is limited. Thinking about what you're giving up, and planning where each portion goes, both lead to smarter decisions.

slides.title: How are short-term and long-term goals different?
slides.text: A short-term goal may take days or weeks, while a long-term goal may take months or years. Saving $30 for headphones needs a different plan from saving $300 for a bike. Longer goals usually need more patience, tracking, and protection from impulse spending.

widgetConfig.scenario: Saving $30 for headphones versus $300 for a bike. Do these need the same plan?

options.label: No — longer goals usually need more patience and tracking
options.outcome: Exactly right! A short-term goal may take days or weeks, while a long-term goal may take months or years, usually needing more patience and tracking.

options.label: Yes, every goal needs exactly the same plan
options.outcome: Goals of different sizes don't need exactly the same plan — a bigger, longer goal usually needs more patience and tracking.

options.label: The size of a goal never affects how you should plan for it
options.outcome: The size of a goal actually affects planning a lot — bigger, longer goals need more patience and tracking.

slides.title: Can gratitude change the way you spend?
slides.text: Yes. Appreciating what you already have can reduce the feeling that you always need the next new thing. Before buying, ask whether the purchase solves a real problem or whether you are simply bored with something that still works.

widgetConfig.scenario: You feel grateful for what you already have, rather than focused on what's new. How might this affect your spending?

options.label: You may feel less need to constantly buy new things
options.outcome: Exactly! Appreciating what you already have can reduce the urge to always chase the next new purchase.

options.label: It has no effect on spending at all
options.outcome: Gratitude actually can shift spending habits — appreciating what you have can reduce the urge to buy more.

options.label: It makes you want to spend even more
options.outcome: Gratitude tends to reduce the urge to spend on new things, not increase it.

slides.title: What can your giving choices say about you?
slides.text: Where you choose to give often reflects what you care about. Someone who loves animals might donate to a shelter, while someone who values education might support a school drive. Giving turns values into action.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone who loves animals donates to a shelter. What does this choice reflect?

options.label: What they care about
options.outcome: Exactly right! Where you choose to give often reflects what you care about — giving turns values into action.

options.label: Nothing — giving choices never reflect anything
options.outcome: Giving choices actually reflect a lot — they turn what you care about into real action.

options.label: Giving choices are always completely random
options.outcome: Giving choices usually aren't random — they often reflect what someone genuinely cares about.

slides.title: What can a spending review teach you?
slides.text: Looking back at a week or month of purchases can reveal patterns you missed in the moment. You may discover that several $3 snacks became $30. The goal is not to feel guilty—it is to use the information to make a better plan next time.

widgetConfig.scenario: You look back and discover several $3 snacks became $30. What's the point of noticing this?

options.label: To use the information to make a better plan next time
options.outcome: Exactly right! The goal of a spending review isn't to feel guilty — it's to use the information to make a better plan next time.

options.label: To feel guilty with no useful purpose
options.outcome: The point isn't to feel guilty — it's to use what you learn to make a better plan going forward.

options.label: Looking back at spending never reveals anything useful
options.outcome: Looking back at spending actually reveals a lot — patterns you missed in the moment, like small snacks adding up.

slides.title: How can you turn a big goal into a plan?
slides.text: Start with the total amount, choose a target date, and work backward. If you need $120 in 12 weeks, saving $10 each week gets you there. Breaking a big number into small steps makes progress easier to measure.

widgetConfig.prompt: Tap the steps in the right order
items: Work backward to a weekly amount

slides.title: What can knock a savings goal off track?
slides.text: Unplanned purchases, forgetting to track spending, or saving only “whatever is left” can slow a goal down. Protect your goal by moving savings first and deciding ahead how much is safe to spend.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're saving for a $50 game, but you keep buying small snacks and little extras along the way. What's happening to your goal?

options.label: Small, frequent purchases can add up and slow down a bigger savings goal
options.outcome: Exactly — small purchases don't feel like much individually, but they add up and can seriously delay a bigger goal.

options.label: Small purchases don't affect big goals at all
options.outcome: They actually do add up — even small, frequent spending can meaningfully slow down progress toward a bigger goal.

options.label: The game price must have gone up
options.outcome: The more likely explanation is that small spending along the way has been eating into the savings — tracking it can help.

slides.title: Why celebrate progress before reaching the finish line?
slides.text: Long goals can feel far away, so noticing milestones keeps motivation alive. If your goal is $200, reaching $50, $100, and $150 are real wins. Celebrate the progress without spending the money you are trying to save.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're halfway to a big savings goal but still have a long way to go. Should you wait until the very end to feel good about it?

options.label: No — celebrating progress along the way helps keep you motivated
options.outcome: Exactly! Recognizing progress, even midway, helps keep your motivation up for the rest of the journey.

options.label: Yes, only the final result matters
options.outcome: Waiting until the very end to feel good can make a long goal feel discouraging — celebrating progress along the way helps keep motivation up.

options.label: Progress doesn't matter at all
options.outcome: Progress matters a lot for staying motivated — celebrating small milestones helps you keep going.

slides.title: How can you know where a donation goes?
slides.text: Before giving, look at what the organization says it does with donations and whether it clearly explains its work. If you donate to a food bank, for example, your money may help buy meals or supplies. Understanding the impact makes giving more intentional.

widgetConfig.scenario: Before donating to a food bank, what should you check?

options.label: What the organization says it does with donations
options.outcome: Exactly right! Looking at what the organization says it does with donations, and whether it clearly explains its work, makes giving more intentional.

options.label: Nothing — donations never need any research
options.outcome: Donations actually benefit from a bit of research — understanding where the money goes makes giving more intentional.

options.label: All organizations use donations in exactly the same way
options.outcome: Organizations don't all use donations the same way — checking what a specific one does helps you give more intentionally.

slides.title: Is it okay to change a money goal?
slides.text: Yes. Goals should match what matters to you now. If you started saving for a gadget but later decide a class or trip matters more, you can redirect the money. Changing a goal thoughtfully is different from abandoning every goal on impulse.

widgetConfig.scenario: You started saving for a gadget but a trip matters more to you now. What can you do?

options.label: Thoughtfully redirect the money toward the new goal
options.outcome: Exactly right! Goals should match what matters to you now — changing a goal thoughtfully is different from abandoning every goal on impulse.

options.label: Never change a goal once it is set
options.outcome: Goals don't have to be permanent — you can thoughtfully redirect your saving if something else now matters more.

options.label: Changing a goal always means giving up on saving entirely
options.outcome: Changing a goal thoughtfully isn't giving up — it's redirecting your saving toward what matters to you now.

quiz.question: Why do long-term goals need different planning than short-term goals?
choices: They take longer and need more patience and planning
They need no planning at all
quiz.explanation: A short-term goal, like a 20-point toy, might take just two weeks to save for. A long-term goal, like a 200-point bike, might take most of a year, so it needs more patience and a steadier plan.

quiz.question: How does gratitude relate to money?
choices: Appreciating what you have tends to bring more satisfaction than chasing more
Gratitude has nothing to do with money
quiz.explanation: Being thankful for what you already have, instead of constantly wanting the next thing, tends to make people more satisfied with their money. Someone who appreciates the bike they own usually feels happier than someone eyeing the next purchase.

quiz.question: What can reviewing your past spending reveal?
choices: Patterns you didn't notice while spending
Nothing useful — spending logs are pointless
quiz.explanation: Looking back at a month of spending often shows patterns you didn't notice while you were actually buying things. You might discover you spent more on snacks than you realized, which helps you plan better next month.

quiz.question: What can your giving choices reveal?
choices: What causes or things matter to you
Giving reveals nothing about a person
quiz.explanation: The causes you choose to donate to say something about what matters to you, just like your spending choices do. Someone who cares about animals might set aside money each month for a shelter instead of spending it all on themselves.

quiz.question: Why break a big goal into smaller steps?
choices: It makes the goal feel less overwhelming and easier to track
Breaking goals into steps makes them harder to reach
quiz.explanation: A big goal, like saving 200 points, can feel impossible all at once. Breaking it into smaller weekly steps, like 20 points a week, makes it feel manageable and easier to track.

quiz.question: What commonly derails a savings goal?
choices: Small unplanned purchases adding up
Goals are never derailed once you set them
quiz.explanation: Small, unplanned purchases, like a snack here and a sticker there, are one of the most common reasons a savings goal takes longer than expected. Noticing your own patterns helps protect a goal you care about.

quiz.question: Why notice progress toward a goal, not just the finish line?
choices: It helps you stay motivated during a long goal
Progress along the way doesn't matter at all
quiz.explanation: Celebrating being halfway to a goal, not just reaching the very end, helps you stay motivated when saving takes a while. Noticing small wins along the way keeps a long goal feeling worth the effort.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to know where a donation goes?
choices: It can make giving feel more meaningful and intentional
It's better to never think about where money goes
quiz.explanation: Knowing that a donation goes directly to a shelter or food bank, and actually helps people or animals, can make giving feel more meaningful. Understanding the impact makes it feel like more than just handing over money.

quiz.question: Is it okay to change a savings goal you set months ago?
choices: Yes, goals can change as what matters to you changes
No, a goal can never be changed once it's set
quiz.explanation: What mattered to you months ago, like a certain toy, might not matter as much now. Checking in on your goals occasionally keeps your saving pointed at something you still genuinely want.

quiz.question: What do gratitude and reviewing your spending have in common?
choices: Both help you feel more satisfied and in control of your money
They have no connection to each other
quiz.explanation: Both practices build awareness about your money instead of letting habits run on autopilot. Appreciating what you have and checking where your money went both help you feel more satisfied and in control.

slides.title: How can skills affect what you earn?
slides.text: Pay is often connected to the value, scarcity, and difficulty of the skills someone can offer. Learning coding, design, sales, repair, writing, or another in-demand skill can create more ways to earn. Building skill is a long-term investment in your future options.

widgetConfig.scenario: A job that requires a rare, difficult skill often pays more than one that doesn't. Why?

options.label: Pay is often connected to the value, scarcity, and difficulty of the skill
options.outcome: Exactly! Pay is often connected to the value, scarcity, and difficulty of the skill a job requires.

options.label: Pay has nothing to do with skill
options.outcome: Pay actually connects closely to skill — rarer, harder skills often come with higher pay.

options.label: All jobs pay exactly the same no matter the skill required
options.outcome: Jobs don't all pay the same — skill level, scarcity, and difficulty all affect pay.

slides.title: What is the difference between gross pay and net pay?
slides.text: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions; net pay is what reaches your bank account after taxes and other deductions. If a paycheck shows $600 gross and $510 deposited, $510 is your net pay. Budget from net pay, because that is the money you actually receive.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your paycheck shows one number before deductions and a smaller number after. Which is net pay?

options.label: The smaller number — what reaches your bank account after deductions
options.outcome: Exactly right! Net pay is what reaches your bank account after deductions, while gross pay is the amount before deductions.

options.label: The bigger number before any deductions
options.outcome: That's gross pay, not net pay — net pay is the smaller amount that actually reaches your bank account.

options.label: There's no real difference between the two
options.outcome: There is a real difference — gross pay is before deductions, and net pay is what actually reaches your account.

slides.title: Why are taxes taken from earnings and purchases?
slides.text: Taxes are collected by governments to fund public services such as roads, schools, emergency services, and other shared programs. The exact taxes you pay depend on where you live, what you earn, and what you buy. A pay stub and receipt can show some of these amounts.

widgetConfig.scenario: Taxes fund things like roads and schools. Who decides and collects them?

options.label: Governments, to fund shared public services
options.outcome: Exactly right! Taxes are collected by governments to fund public services such as roads, schools, and emergency services.

options.label: No one — taxes serve no real purpose
options.outcome: Taxes actually serve a real purpose — funding shared public services like roads and schools.

options.label: Taxes are always exactly the same everywhere
options.outcome: Taxes actually vary quite a bit — the exact amounts depend on where you live, what you earn, and what you buy.

slides.title: What does “pay yourself first” mean?
slides.text: It means moving money to savings before you start spending the rest. If you earn $100 and decide to save 20%, move $20 first and treat the remaining $80 as available to spend. This turns saving from a leftover into a priority.

widgetConfig.scenario: You get your paycheck and plan to pay bills, spend some on fun stuff, and save whatever is left over — but there's rarely anything left. What's a better approach?

options.label: Move money into savings first, before spending on anything else
options.outcome: Exactly — "pay yourself first" means treating savings like a required bill, not an afterthought. That way saving actually happens instead of hoping for leftovers.

options.label: Keep spending first and hope something's left for savings
options.outcome: That approach is why savings often ends up at $0 — there's rarely much left after spending happens first.

options.label: Only save if you get a bonus
options.outcome: Waiting for bonuses means missing consistent saving opportunities — paying yourself first from every paycheck builds savings more reliably.

slides.title: Why do different jobs pay different amounts?
slides.text: Wages can be affected by skill level, training, experience, supply and demand, location, risk, responsibility, and the employer. A job that requires years of specialized training may pay differently from an entry-level job. Pay is shaped by several factors, not just effort.

widgetConfig.scenario: A job requiring years of specialized training pays differently from an entry-level job. Is pay based only on effort?

options.label: No — skill, training, experience, and other factors matter too
options.outcome: Exactly right! Wages can be affected by skill level, training, experience, supply and demand, location, and more — pay is shaped by several factors, not just effort.

options.label: Yes, pay is based only on how hard someone works
options.outcome: Pay isn't based only on effort — skill level, training, and other factors shape wages too.

options.label: Pay is always completely random with no real factors
options.outcome: Pay isn't random — it's shaped by real factors like skill level, training, experience, and location.

slides.title: What is a side hustle or freelance work?
slides.text: A side hustle is extra income earned outside a main job, while freelance work usually means being paid per project or service rather than as a regular employee. Examples include tutoring, pet sitting, design, coding, or selling handmade items. Income may vary, so planning matters.

widgetConfig.scenario: You tutor or pet sit on the side, outside your main job. What is this called?

options.label: A side hustle or freelance work
options.outcome: Exactly right! A side hustle is extra income earned outside a main job, and freelance work usually means being paid per project rather than as a regular employee.

options.label: This has no name and is not a real thing
options.outcome: This actually has a clear name and is very real — it's called a side hustle or freelance work.

options.label: This only counts if it is your only source of income
options.outcome: A side hustle is specifically extra income outside a main job, not necessarily your only source.

slides.title: How do you read a pay stub?
slides.text: A pay stub usually shows hours or salary, gross pay, taxes and other deductions, and net pay. Read it to check whether the hours, pay rate, and deductions make sense. Understanding your pay stub helps you catch errors and know where your earnings go.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your pay stub shows your gross pay is $500 but your actual deposit is $420. What explains the difference?

options.label: Taxes and other deductions were taken out before the deposit
options.outcome: Exactly — the difference between gross pay (before deductions) and net pay (what you actually receive) usually comes from taxes and other withholdings.

options.label: The employer made a mistake
options.outcome: This is usually completely normal — the gap between gross and net pay comes from taxes and other standard deductions, not an error.

options.label: You're being underpaid
options.outcome: This gap is typically normal and expected — it reflects taxes and deductions, not necessarily being underpaid.

slides.title: Why automate savings?
slides.text: Automatic transfers move money to savings without requiring a fresh decision every payday. If $25 automatically moves to savings each time you are paid, you are less likely to spend it first. Automation can make a good habit easier to maintain.

widgetConfig.scenario: $25 automatically moves to savings each payday. Why might this help?

options.label: You're less likely to spend it first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Automatic transfers move money to savings without requiring a fresh decision every payday, making you less likely to spend it first.

options.label: Automating savings never actually helps
options.outcome: Automating savings actually helps a lot — it can make a good habit easier to maintain.

options.label: This only works if you remember to do it manually every time
options.outcome: The whole point of automating is that you don't need to remember — it happens without a fresh decision each payday.

slides.title: How can investing in yourself pay off?
slides.text: Money and time spent on useful education, certifications, tools, or practice can increase your future opportunities. A course is not automatically valuable, though—compare its cost with the skills, credibility, and opportunities it may realistically provide.

widgetConfig.scenario: You spend money on a useful course or certification. Is every course automatically worth the cost?

options.label: No — compare its cost with the skills and opportunities it provides
options.outcome: Exactly right! Money and time spent on useful education can increase future opportunities, but a course isn't automatically valuable — compare cost with what it realistically provides.

options.label: Yes, any course is always worth any price
options.outcome: Not every course is automatically worth its price — comparing the cost with the real skills and opportunities it provides matters.

options.label: Investing in yourself never pays off in the future
options.outcome: Investing in yourself actually can pay off quite a bit, when the cost matches the real value it provides.

quiz.question: How does developing valuable skills affect earning potential?
choices: More valuable skills typically lead to more ways to earn
Skills have no connection to earning money
quiz.explanation: Skills that are genuinely useful to others, like coding or design, tend to open up more ways to earn money over time. Someone with a marketable skill usually has more income options than someone with the same free time but fewer developed abilities.

quiz.question: What's the difference between gross pay and net pay?
choices: Net pay is what's left after taxes and deductions
They always mean the exact same amount
quiz.explanation: Gross pay is the full amount a job pays before anything is subtracted, while net pay is what actually lands in your account after taxes and deductions. A job paying $15 an hour might only deposit about $12 an hour once taxes are taken out.

quiz.question: What do taxes generally pay for?
choices: Shared things like roads, schools, and public services
They disappear and pay for nothing
quiz.explanation: Taxes are money collected from earnings or purchases that governments use to fund shared things like roads, schools, and public services. Part of the price on a store receipt is usually sales tax, which goes toward resources the whole community relies on.

quiz.question: What does "pay yourself first" mean?
choices: Saving a portion of money right away, before spending on anything else
Spending everything first and saving whatever happens to be left
quiz.explanation: Paying yourself first means setting aside a portion of any money you earn for savings immediately, before spending on anything else. Saving 20% of every paycheck the moment it arrives makes saving automatic instead of whatever happens to be left over.

quiz.question: Why do some jobs pay more than others?
choices: They may require rarer skills or more risk and responsibility
All jobs are required by law to pay the same
quiz.explanation: Pay often reflects supply and demand: jobs that require rare, hard-to-learn skills or involve more risk and responsibility tend to pay more than jobs almost anyone can do with little training. This can help guide which skills are worth developing.

quiz.question: What is a 'side hustle'?
choices: Extra income earned outside a traditional job, like freelance work
A type of tax that only adults pay
quiz.explanation: A side hustle is extra income earned outside a traditional job, such as tutoring, selling crafts, or freelance design, usually on a flexible schedule. It can supplement a main income or help build a skill into something bigger.

quiz.question: What does a pay stub show?
choices: Gross pay, deductions, and final net pay
Only how many hours you worked, nothing else
quiz.explanation: A pay stub is a document that lists your gross pay, each individual deduction like taxes, and the final net pay you actually receive. Reading it carefully gives a full, honest picture of where your earned money actually goes.

quiz.question: Why automate a transfer to savings each payday?
choices: It removes the temptation to spend that money first
Automatic transfers are riskier than doing it manually
quiz.explanation: Setting up an automatic transfer to savings the moment you're paid removes the temptation to spend that money on something else first. It turns the intention of 'pay yourself first' into a dependable habit that doesn't rely on willpower alone.

quiz.question: How can learning a new skill be a kind of investment?
choices: It can increase what you're able to earn later
Skills have no effect on future earning
quiz.explanation: Spending time or money on a certification, class, or new skill is a form of investing in yourself, since it can increase your future earning potential. Not all valuable investments are purely financial — some pay off through skills and opportunities.

quiz.question: What connects taxes and net pay?
choices: Taxes are one of the deductions that turn gross pay into net pay
Taxes and net pay are completely unrelated
quiz.explanation: Taxes are one of several deductions, alongside things like retirement contributions, that get subtracted from gross pay to produce net pay. That's part of why a $15-an-hour job doesn't put a full $15 into your account each hour.

slides.title: What are credit and debt?
slides.text: Credit is the ability to borrow money with an agreement to repay it; debt is the amount you currently owe. Borrowing can be useful, but interest and fees can make the final cost higher than the original purchase. Always understand the repayment terms before using credit.

widgetConfig.scenario: You borrow money and agree to repay it with interest. What's the real cost?

options.label: Possibly more than the original purchase, due to interest and fees
options.outcome: Exactly right! Credit is the ability to borrow money with an agreement to repay it, but interest and fees can make the final cost higher than the original purchase.

options.label: Always exactly the same as the original purchase
options.outcome: The real cost can be higher than the original purchase, once interest and fees are included.

options.label: Credit never involves understanding repayment terms
options.outcome: Credit actually requires understanding repayment terms — that's essential before using it.

slides.title: What should you know about buy now, pay later?
slides.text: Buy now, pay later splits a purchase into several payments, which can make an expensive item feel cheaper than it is. The full price has not changed, and missed payments may lead to fees or other consequences depending on the service. Track every payment before committing.

widgetConfig.scenario: A "buy now, pay later" app lets you get a $200 item for 4 easy payments of $50. It feels affordable. What should you consider before using it?

options.label: Whether you can actually afford all 4 payments, not just the first one
options.outcome: Smart thinking — buy now, pay later can feel like free money upfront, but it's still real debt, and missing payments can bring fees or hurt your credit.

options.label: Nothing, since it's broken into small payments it's basically free
options.outcome: It's not free — it's still debt, just split up. Missing a payment can bring real fees and consequences.

options.label: It's always a bad idea no matter what
options.outcome: It's not always bad if used carefully — the key is making sure you can truly afford every payment, not just the first one.

slides.title: Why should you watch recurring costs?
slides.text: A few monthly subscriptions can become a large yearly expense. Three subscriptions costing $10 each are $30 a month, or $360 a year. Reviewing recurring charges helps you decide whether each service still earns its place in your budget.

widgetConfig.scenario: You signed up for three different subscriptions months ago and forgot about two of them. What's the lesson here?

options.label: Small recurring costs can add up unnoticed over time
options.outcome: Exactly — subscriptions and recurring costs are easy to forget, but they keep charging you every month. Periodically reviewing them can save real money.

options.label: Subscriptions never actually cost much
options.outcome: Even small subscriptions add up significantly over months and years — it's worth periodically reviewing what you're actually paying for.

options.label: It's impossible to track recurring costs
options.outcome: You can track them — periodically reviewing your bank or card statements helps you notice forgotten subscriptions.

slides.title: How can peer pressure affect spending?
slides.text: Friends, trends, and social media can make a purchase feel necessary even when it is not. Before spending, ask, “Would I still want this if nobody else saw it?” That question can separate your own preferences from pressure to keep up.

widgetConfig.scenario: A purchase feels necessary because of trends and friends. What question can help separate real preference from pressure?

options.label: "Would I still want this if nobody else saw it?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! This question can separate your own preferences from pressure to keep up with friends, trends, or social media.

options.label: No question can ever help with this
options.outcome: A thoughtful question actually can help a lot — it separates your real preferences from outside pressure.

options.label: Peer pressure never actually affects spending
options.outcome: Peer pressure actually can affect spending quite a bit — a thoughtful question helps you notice and separate from it.

slides.title: What does a credit score represent?
slides.text: A credit score is a number created from information in a credit report, such as payment history and amounts owed. Lenders may use it when deciding whether to lend and what terms to offer. Building healthy credit starts with understanding agreements and paying obligations on time.

widgetConfig.scenario: A number is created from your payment history and amounts owed. What is this called?

options.label: A credit score
options.outcome: Exactly right! A credit score is a number created from information in a credit report, which lenders may use when deciding whether to lend.

options.label: A lucky number with no real meaning
options.outcome: This isn't just a lucky number — it's a real score based on payment history and amounts owed, called a credit score.

options.label: This has nothing to do with borrowing money
options.outcome: This actually is directly connected to borrowing money — lenders use it to decide whether and on what terms to lend.

slides.title: How can interest help you or hurt you?
slides.text: Interest is the cost of borrowing or the money you may earn on savings. If you borrow, interest can make you repay more than you received. If you save in an interest-paying account, interest can add to your balance over time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Interest applies both to borrowing and to savings. Can it work both ways?

options.label: Yes — it can cost you more when borrowing, or add to savings
options.outcome: Exactly right! If you borrow, interest can make you repay more than you received; if you save, interest can add to your balance over time.

options.label: No, interest only ever costs you money
options.outcome: Interest doesn't only cost you money — it can also add to your balance when you're saving.

options.label: Interest never has any real effect either way
options.outcome: Interest actually has a real effect both ways — it can cost you more when borrowing or add to your savings.

slides.title: What are warning signs of a bad financial deal?
slides.text: Be cautious when someone pressures you to act immediately, hides important details, promises something that sounds unrealistic, or makes the terms hard to understand. A legitimate decision should survive questions, comparison, and time to think.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone offers you an investment opportunity and insists you decide right now or you'll miss out. Is this a warning sign?

options.label: Yes — pressure to act immediately is a classic red flag
options.outcome: Exactly! Legitimate opportunities rarely require an instant decision — pressure to rush is a major warning sign of a scam.

options.label: No, urgency just means it's a great opportunity
options.outcome: Urgency is actually one of the most common scam tactics — real opportunities don't usually require instant decisions.

options.label: It only matters if they also ask for money upfront
options.outcome: Pressure to act immediately is a red flag on its own, even before any money changes hands.

slides.title: What is lifestyle inflation?
slides.text: Lifestyle inflation happens when spending rises almost as fast as income. Someone gets a raise, then immediately upgrades meals, clothes, subscriptions, and gadgets, leaving no extra savings. Increasing savings along with income can help prevent this pattern.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone gets a raise and immediately upgrades meals, clothes, and subscriptions, leaving no extra savings. What is this pattern called?

options.label: Lifestyle inflation
options.outcome: Exactly right! Lifestyle inflation happens when spending rises almost as fast as income, leaving no extra savings — increasing savings along with income can help prevent this.

options.label: Smart budgeting
options.outcome: This isn't smart budgeting — spending rising to match every raise, with no extra savings, is called lifestyle inflation.

options.label: This pattern has no name and never actually happens
